entries.lesson_core_move: Characterize the unit impulse by using its zero-width, unit-area behavior to treat delta(t) as the impulse building block for continuous-time signal descriptions.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Definition of the Unit Impulse
sections.learning_goal: Define the unit impulse as a generalized continuous-time signal with point support and fixed unit area, and distinguish that definition from ordinary pointwise signal values.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; this section is defined purely from symbolic and verbal characterization.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Anchor the core meaning of $\delta(t)$ as a zero-width signal of unit area: $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\delta(t)\,dt=1$, and treat it as the continuous-time impulse building block.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Start with a narrow pulse approximation $\delta_\epsilon(t)=\frac{1}{\epsilon}\,u(t+\epsilon/2)-\frac{1}{\epsilon}\,u(t-\epsilon/2)$, then read the limiting behavior as $\epsilon\to 0^+$.
paragraph_plan: Open with the intuitive conflict: ordinary functions have widths and finite heights, while the impulse is a point-concentrated limiting concept.
Define support and point behavior by stating that the signal is concentrated at $t=0$ and is identified via its area action, not by ordinary pointwise value.
State the two defining properties together: $\delta(t)=0$ for $t\ne 0$ and $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\delta(t)\,dt=1$.
Connect to active instruction cycles: present one controlled check from a limiting rectangle to fix the mental model before practice begins.

entries.lesson_core_move: Distinguish impulse area from ordinary signal amplitude when interpreting unit impulse terms in continuous-time signal constructions.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Impulse Area vs. Impulse Amplitude
sections.learning_goal: Establish that coefficients in impulse terms denote area (weight), not pointwise sample value, and that this weight is preserved under shifts.

question_policy.practice_question_model: not-applicable

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Define the unit impulse with zero-width but finite area and state that the coefficient in $A\delta(t-t_0)$ is an impulse area parameter.
paragraph_plan: Open with the core distinction: regular signals have pointwise values, while impulse terms model concentrated area on the time axis.
State the unit-impulse normalization and show why the shift parameter $t_0$ does not change the impulse area.
Introduce signed coefficients and connect them to positive, negative, or zero area in a signal representation.
Contrast this with ordinary amplitude by comparing one ordinary step value and one impulse term side-by-side.
Preview that later examples will use this rule to read and write impulse-based constructions.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the tutorial symbolic and short; avoid graph-first explanations here so questions can stay pure symbolic in the first section.

sections.section_title: Identifying Area as the Quantity Assigned to an Impulse
sections.learning_goal: Given a symbolic impulse term, compute the impulse area directly from its coefficient and report sign accurately.

question_policy.practice_question_model: For $y(t)=4\delta(t-2)$, what is the impulse area contributed by this term?
distractor_plan: Treat $4\delta(t-2)$ as if value $4$ is pointwise amplitude and then ignore area interpretation.
Compute area as one even when the coefficient is negative, missing signed area.
Use shift $t_0=2$ as if it scaled the area.
Confuse $\delta(t-2)$ with a step and answer with an interval length.
Report the wrong area due to using $\delta(t-2)=2$ instead of integrating the term.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Find the impulse area for each term in $x(t)=3\delta(t)+2\delta(t-1)-\delta(t+1)$.

example_outline.variation_from_previous: Extends the tutorial base case by using multiple shifted terms and a negative coefficient.
solution_step_plan: Identify each impulse term separately as $A\delta(t-t_0)$.
Use $\int A\delta(t-t_0)dt=A$ for each coefficient $A$.
Preserve sign and match each area value to its time location.
Check whether any coefficient is zero, which would imply no impulse area at that term.
practice_variation_axes: Change coefficients while keeping shifts fixed.
Change shifts while preserving coefficients.
Introduce one negative coefficient and one larger magnitude coefficient.

sections.section_title: Distinguishing Impulse Area from Ordinary Signal Amplitude

example_outline.variation_from_previous: Combines multiple single-term patterns and scales into a full-termwise parsing exercise.
solution_step_plan: Split the expression into each shifted-impulse term.
For each term, solve its argument equation for activation time.
Pair each solved time with its corresponding coefficient.

Sign patterns of location and coefficients

entries.lesson_title: Multiplying a Function by an Impulse
entries.lesson_core_move: Reduce a product f(t)delta(t) to f(0)delta(t) by recognizing that the impulse keeps only the function value at t = 0.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Multiplying a Function by an Impulse
sections.learning_goal: State and apply the rule that $f(t)\delta(t)=f(0)\delta(t)$ because the impulse keeps only the value at $t=0$.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the core move is symbolic substitution and simplification.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Keep this section text-only with formulas only.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Introduce the key identity $f(t)\delta(t)=f(0)\delta(t)$ and why it is the only mechanism needed for products with $\delta(t)$.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Use the base simplification of $\left(2t+3\right)\delta(t)$ by evaluating $f(0)=3$.
paragraph_plan: State that $\delta(t)$ is an idealized point operation that samples the multiplier at $t=0$.
Write the target identity as a rule for all symbolic multipliers: $f(t)\delta(t)=f(0)\delta(t)$.
Show two substitutions: one nonzero coefficient and one zero-weight factor.
Show that this rule is used identically for constants, polynomials, and later non-polynomial multipliers.

solution_step_plan: Introduce direct substitution framework from the identity.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep this as minimal direct instruction with no image. Do not include questions in this section.

sections.section_title: Evaluating f(0) in a Product f(t)delta(t)
sections.learning_goal: Evaluate $f(0)$ from an algebraic multiplier and rewrite the full product into a sampled impulse form.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; all steps are symbolic.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate graphs or signal plots for this section.

question_policy.practice_question_model: Given an algebraic $f(t)$, evaluate $f(0)$ and simplify $f(t)\delta(t)$ to the correct sampled form.
distractor_plan: Keep $t$ in the final coefficient instead of replacing it with $0$.
Evaluate at $t=1$ or another value instead of $t=0$.
Leave the expression as $f(t)\delta(t)$ instead of reducing it.
Drop the coefficient and return only $\delta(t)$ when it should be scaled.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Simplify $\left(4t+1\right)\delta(t)$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Demonstrate direct substitution $f(0)=1$ and rewrite as $1\delta(t)=\delta(t)$.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Starts the example sequence by adding one non-constant factor, while preserving the same sampling rule from the tutorial.
solution_step_plan: Set $f(t)=4t+1$.
Compute $f(0)=4\cdot 0+1=1$.
Use the identity to write $\left(4t+1\right)\delta(t)=f(0)\delta(t)=1\delta(t)=\delta(t)$.
practice_variation_axes: Vary polynomial coefficients while keeping a single substitution at zero.
Swap addition and subtraction forms.
Include negative and fractional constants in $f(t)$.

sections.handoff_notes: Model question and distractors should stay algebraic and one-step substitution based.

sections.section_title: Simplifying Algebraic Factors Multiplying delta(t)
sections.learning_goal: Handle factored polynomial multipliers by evaluating each factor at zero before collapsing to the final coefficient.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; all simplification is symbolic.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: No signal diagram or graph is needed.

question_policy.practice_question_model: Given a factored polynomial multiplier, evaluate each factor at zero and simplify the product with $\delta(t)$.
distractor_plan: Evaluate only one factor and ignore the rest.
Multiply as if the function were evaluated at $t=1$.
Confuse $0\delta(t)$ with $\delta(t)$.
Expand with arithmetic mistakes before substitution.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Simplify $(2t-3)(t+5)\delta(t)$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Demonstrate factor-wise sampling at zero and multiplication of sampled factors.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Adds two-factor structure to force controlled growth from single-factor polynomials.
solution_step_plan: Evaluate at zero: $(2\cdot 0-3)=-3$, $(0+5)=5$.
Return $-15\delta(t)$ as the simplified product.
practice_variation_axes: Vary factor signs and ordering.
Introduce higher-degree factors while keeping one substitution.
Include one $t$-only factor to test automatic zero detection.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the pattern tightly controlled: evaluate each factor at $0$, then combine into a coefficient.

sections.section_title: Simplifying Exponential and Sinusoidal Factors Multiplying delta(t)
sections.learning_goal: Extend the same sampling identity to exponential and sinusoidal multipliers.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; non-polynomial cases are still symbolic substitution.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: No graph-based representation requested.

question_policy.practice_question_model: Evaluate a product of exponential and trigonometric factors at $t=0$ and simplify the impulse product.
distractor_plan: Use value of trig functions at a wrong angle.
Evaluate $e^{at}$ incorrectly as $a$ at zero.
Multiply wrong sign from sampled trig value.
Keep a factor of $t$ in the final expression.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Simplify $5e^{-2t}\sin(\pi t)\delta(t)$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that sampling non-polynomial factors still uses $t=0$, giving a zero product in this case.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Adds mixed transcendent multipliers while preserving the same evaluate-at-zero procedure.
solution_step_plan: Set $f(t)=5e^{-2t}\sin(\pi t)$.
Compute $f(0)=5\cdot e^0\cdot \sin(0)=0$.
Conclude $5e^{-2t}\sin(\pi t)\delta(t)=0\delta(t)=0$.
practice_variation_axes: Replace sine with cosine and vary phase constants.
Replace $e^{-2t}$ with $e^{at}$ for different $a$.
Use expressions that evaluate to nonzero at zero for contrast.

sections.handoff_notes: Emphasize that standard-function values are known at zero constants, not integrated or approximated.

sections.section_title: Recognizing Zero-Weight Products with delta(t)
sections.learning_goal: Develop the recognition pattern that any factor containing $t$ as a multiplier evaluates to zero at the impulse location.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; this section is purely rule-checking by substitution.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not use visuals; this is a symbolic edge-case checkpoint.

question_policy.practice_question_model: Determine if a multiplier with explicit $t$ factors gives zero or nonzero when multiplied by $\delta(t)$.
distractor_plan: Treat $t\delta(t)$ as $\delta(t)$ instead of $0$.
Evaluate a shifted-like factor at the wrong location.
Choose a nonzero coefficient by dropping explicit $t$ terms.
Assume any product with $\delta(t)$ is automatically nonzero unless coefficient is visibly zero by inspection.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Simplify $t(2t+1)(t-4)\delta(t)$ and decide whether the result is zero.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Check the sampled factor and return either $0$ or a scaled impulse based on $f(0)$.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Introduces a zero-weight trap using explicit $t$ factors, which is the most common extension before shifted-impulse topics.
solution_step_plan: Evaluate $f(0)=0\cdot1\cdot(-4)=0$.
Return $0\delta(t)=0$ and state the general shortcut: if $t$ multiplies the impulse at $t=0$, the term vanishes.
practice_variation_axes: Switch between zero-weight and nonzero examples.
Use mixed shifted-like expressions with and without explicit $t$ factors.
Use coefficients and constants to create close distractor patterns.

sections.handoff_notes: This is the final control checkpoint before shifted-impulse lessons; generate one direct-zero and one near-zero distractor set in questions.

entries.lesson_title: Multiplying a Function by a Shifted Impulse
entries.lesson_core_move: Convert f(t)delta(t - t0) into f(t0)delta(t - t0) by evaluating the function at the shifted impulse location.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Multiplying a Function by a Shifted Impulse
sections.learning_goal: State the shifted-impulse substitution rule and use it to simplify products where the only dependence on time is through $f(t)$ and the $\delta$ argument $t-t_0$.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image is needed because the target move is a direct symbolic substitution pattern.

question_policy.practice_question_model: not-applicable

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Introduce and justify the one-step rewrite $f(t)\delta(t-t_0)=f(t_0)\delta(t-t_0)$, emphasizing that $\delta$ is nonzero only at $t=t_0$ in symbolic operations.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Show the base simplification $f(t)\delta(t-2)=f(2)\delta(t-2)$ and label this as locating the impulse.
paragraph_plan: Open by naming the known rule for ordinary impulse multiplication and contrast it with the shifted case.
State that the $\delta$ factor forces the surrounding expression to be sampled at $t=t_0$ and that all other $t$ dependence is replaced by $f(t_0)$.
Demonstrate one symbolic rewrite in full and close with a concise check using a different shift value.

sections.section_title: Evaluating a Function at the Impulse Location
sections.learning_goal: Use the substitution rule to evaluate a simple function at the shifted impulse location and rewrite the product as a scaled shifted impulse.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: Symbolic substitution is sufficient; no diagram is required.

question_policy.practice_question_model: Simplify $f(t)\delta(t-3)$ for $f(t)=t^2-2t+1$ and return the scaled $\delta$.
distractor_plan: Wrongly keep the original $f(t)$ instead of evaluating at $t=t_0$.
Use $f(0)$ or another default sample point instead of $t=t_0$.
Drop the $\delta$ location and return a non-shifted impulse.
Change the sign in the $\delta$ argument when applying the sample point.
Compute an incorrect function value from algebraic simplification errors.

paragraph_plan: N/A

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Evaluate and simplify $f(t)\delta(t-5)$ for $f(t)=2t+3$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Produce $13\delta(t-5)$ by substituting $t=5$ into $f(t)$ and preserving the shifted $\delta$ argument.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Applies the tutorial rule to a concrete algebraic function with a nonzero shift and requires an explicit simplification of $f(5)$.
solution_step_plan: Identify $t_0$ from the shifted $\delta$ argument in $\delta(t-t_0)$.
Evaluate the multiplier at that location: $f(5)=2(5)+3=13$.
Rewrite the product as $13\delta(t-5)$ in the final simplified form.
practice_variation_axes: Shift value $t_0$ should vary among positive and negative values.
Function form should vary between polynomial and trigonometric/exponential samples.
Include optional scalar multipliers in front of the product.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the example as a direct substitution drill; this section is the first concrete checkpoint before introducing sign-shift nuances.

sections.section_title: Multiplying by a Shifted Impulse at a Negative Time
sections.learning_goal: Apply the same substitution rule when the shift is negative and prevent common sign errors in locating $t=-t_0$.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: Use symbolic examples only; negative-shift handling is handled by argument parsing.

question_policy.practice_question_model: Simplify $f(t)\delta(t+2)$ for $f(t)=3t-4$.
distractor_plan: Use $+2$ instead of $-2$ when solving for the impulse location.
Evaluate $f(0)$ rather than the shifted location.
Drop the minus sign and return a shifted impulse at the wrong center.
Evaluate incorrectly and get $f(-2)$ vs $f(2)$ reversed.
Keep the original symbolic factor $3t-4$ without evaluation.

paragraph_plan: N/A

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Evaluate $f(t)\delta(t+3)$ for $f(t)=t^2-1$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Produce $8\delta(t+3)$ by correctly identifying the impulse location at $t=-3$ and evaluating $f(-3)$.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Adds the negative-shift wrinkle by requiring substitution at a negative sample point while keeping the same symbolic structure.
solution_step_plan: Read the shifted $\delta$ as $\delta(t-(-3))$ and set the sample point $t=-3$.
Rewrite the product as $8\delta(t+3)$ with unchanged impulse position.
practice_variation_axes: Vary between $\delta(t+a)$ and $\delta(t-a)$ forms.
Use both even and odd polynomials so sign bookkeeping is tested.
Include scalar multipliers to test coefficient propagation.

sections.handoff_notes: Emphasize why $\delta(t+3)$ means $t=-3$, not $t=+3$. Keep one line of algebra only.

sections.section_title: Combining Function Values with Scaled Shifted Impulses
sections.learning_goal: Combine explicit scale factors and evaluated function values at the same shifted impulse location into one impulse coefficient.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No visual artifacts required; coefficient arithmetic is symbolic.

question_policy.practice_question_model: Simplify $-2\delta(t-1)+(3t+1)\delta(t-1)$.
distractor_plan: Keep both shifted impulse terms separate.
Evaluate only one of the shifted impulses and ignore the explicit scalar.
Shift the $\delta$ argument incorrectly during combination.
Combine coefficients but evaluate at the wrong time point.
Preserve a symbolic $t$ term in the final coefficient.

paragraph_plan: N/A

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Simplify $2(4t+2)\delta(t-4)-3\delta(t-4)$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Turn the expression into a single shifted impulse $33\delta(t-4)$ after evaluating $2(4t+2)$ at $t=4$ and combining with the standalone scale.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Introduces coefficient aggregation by merging evaluated function scaling with an explicit impulse weight at the same shift.
solution_step_plan: Apply the shift rule to the first term: $2(4t+2)\delta(t-4)=2(18)\delta(t-4)=36\delta(t-4)$.
Keep $-3\delta(t-4)$ as $-3\delta(t-4)$.
Add coefficients: $36\delta(t-4)-3\delta(t-4)=33\delta(t-4)$.
State the final combined result with the same shift index.
practice_variation_axes: Vary the number and sign of separated coefficients at the same shift.
Vary which term contains the function factor versus constant impulse coefficient.
Vary function complexity so simplification is required after substitution.

sections.handoff_notes: Require explicit confirmation that all terms share identical shift; otherwise do not combine terms into one impulse.

sections.section_title: Multiplying a Piecewise Function by a Shifted Impulse
sections.learning_goal: Evaluate piecewise-defined functions at the impulse location to simplify a product with shifted $\delta$, preserving only the matching branch value.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: The piecewise structure is handled with symbolic branch-selection; no graph needed.

question_policy.practice_question_model: Simplify $(f(t))\delta(t-1)$ where $f(t)=\{t,\, t<0;\, t+4,\, t\ge 0\}$.
distractor_plan: Use the wrong branch of the piecewise function for the substitution point.
Keep the piecewise notation instead of reducing to a single evaluated value.
Return a non-shifted impulse due to forgetting the original argument.
Evaluate an unrelated point (such as $t=0$) instead of the sampled shift.
Preserve a variable $t$ in the final coefficient.

paragraph_plan: N/A

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Simplify $f(t)\delta(t-2)$ for $f(t)=\{t,\, t<1;\, 3-t,\, t\ge 1\}$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Select the correct branch at $t=2$, evaluate $f(2)=1$, and return $1\delta(t-2)$.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Adds a piecewise function wrinkle: select the correct branch at the sample point before simplification.
solution_step_plan: Locate the impulse center: $t_0=2$ from $\delta(t-2)$.
Select the branch for $t=2$ from the piecewise definition to get $f(2)=3-2=1$.
Substitute into the rule and rewrite as $1\delta(t-2)$ (or equivalent scaled form).
practice_variation_axes: Vary boundary conditions ($<$, $\le$, $\ge$) to test branch handling.
Vary branch formulas so learners must compute one expression at the sample point.
Use both positive and negative shifts for piecewise center selection.

sections.handoff_notes: No extra scaffolding beyond branch selection is needed; this is the highest-complexity symbolic extension before moving onward in the module.
